prompt: You find a TRS jack labelled only "OUT" on a piece of gear. Which are documented connection conventions covered in this lesson for a TRS (three-conductor) plug? Select all that apply.

options.text: Balanced mono: tip hot, ring cold, sleeve ground
options.explanation: Correct. This is the usual balanced line connection on 1/4″ TRS.

options.text: Unbalanced stereo: tip left, ring right, sleeve ground
options.explanation: Correct. Headphone and many consumer connections use TRS this way.

options.text: Speaker-level and line-level signals at the same time
options.explanation: This is not one of the documented audio or MIDI connection conventions taught here. A custom pinout must not be assumed from a TRS connector.

options.text: TRS MIDI (Type A or B) on some compact devices
options.explanation: Correct. 3.5 mm TRS jacks are used for MIDI too, which is why labels and manuals matter.

workedExample:
The connector shape doesn't define the signal. A three-conductor jack can be:

| Use | Tip | Ring | Sleeve |
|---|---|---|---|
| Balanced mono | Hot | Cold | Ground |
| Unbalanced stereo | Left | Right | Ground |
| MIDI Type A | Pin 5 | Pin 4 | Pin 2 |

Always check the device documentation. Elektron's manuals, for example, say which Digitakt jacks are balanced and which TRS jack is the stereo headphone output.

prompt: How does a balanced connection reject interference picked up along a cable?

options.text: The shield blocks all interference before it reaches the conductors
options.explanation: The shield helps, but the defining mechanism of balanced audio is common-mode rejection at the receiver.

options.text: The signal is sent at a higher voltage, so interference is relatively smaller
options.explanation: A higher signal voltage is not what defines balance. Noise rejection depends on impedance balance, cable construction and the receiving circuit.

options.text: Interference appears almost equally on hot and cold (common mode), and the receiver amplifies only their difference
options.explanation: Correct in the balanced-line model. Symmetric impedances and suitable cabling make interference predominantly common mode; the differential input rejects it to the extent of its finite common-mode rejection.

options.text: Balanced lines require equal and opposite signals on both conductors, which cancel noise
options.explanation: That is a common misconception. An impedance-balanced output with signal on one leg only is still fully balanced.

workedExample:
1. Hot and cold have equal impedances to ground and run as a twisted pair, so induced noise and ground-voltage differences can appear nearly equally on both.
2. The receiver measures hot − cold.
3. Signal (present as a difference) passes; the equal component of the noise is rejected, within the receiver’s limits.
4. This is why the Digitakt's "impedance balanced" outputs still give the benefit when connected with TRS cables to balanced inputs.
